situation:
You and your teammate are the director of marketing and the manager of client relations at MERIDIAN CLAIMS PARTNERS, a medical billing company that prepares, files, and collects insurance claims for hospitals and physician practices. The company's chief executive officer (judge), hired eleven months ago, has asked the two of you to bring a recommendation to this week's executive meeting.

MERIDIAN CLAIMS PARTNERS sells a service rather than a product, and after two losing years it is rebuilding on that difference. Previous leadership competed on price and lost accounts anyway, and the rebrand is the first chance to credit the account team that held both major clients through the losses. The chief executive officer (judge) has committed the board to one company-wide document destruction schedule by the end of the quarter.

The largest new account, HARBORLINE HEALTH SYSTEM, signed a pilot agreement requiring every claim document to be destroyed eighteen months after the claim closes. Harborline made that promise to its own patients, and no competing billing firm in the region offers it. Extending the same eighteen-month purge to every client would give MERIDIAN CLAIMS PARTNERS a differentiator it could advertise at home and in the overseas markets now shopping for billing partners.

The oldest account, VALE RIDGE ORTHOPEDIC GROUP, signed an agreement requiring every supporting document to be held for seven years so the practice can defend itself in a payer audit. Vale Ridge stayed through both losing years, supplies the endorsement the rebuild's marketing rests on, and is roughly a sixth of revenue. Some claims are billed for both clients, since Vale Ridge surgeons operate inside Harborline facilities, and one record cannot follow both schedules.

The chief executive officer (judge) wants the two of you to analyze the choices and recommend one. Standardizing on the eighteen-month purge means telling Vale Ridge its audit protection ends, and likely losing that account, its endorsement, and its share of revenue. Standardizing on seven-year retention means telling Harborline the purge promise will not outlive the pilot, giving up the one claim no rival offers. Keeping both schedules means paying for duplicate systems and staff during a turnaround, with no single promise to advertise.

You will present your recommendation to the chief executive officer (judge) in a meeting to take place in the executive office. The chief executive officer (judge) will begin the meeting by greeting you and asking to hear your ideas. After you have presented and have answered the chief executive officer's (judge) questions, the chief executive officer (judge) will thank you for your work.
judgeCharacterization:
You are the chief executive officer (judge) of MERIDIAN CLAIMS PARTNERS, and you were hired eleven months ago to turn the company around. Business background is the same as the situation above. You have told the board that the company will operate one document destruction schedule by the end of the quarter, and the director of marketing and the manager of client relations are bringing you their recommendation for what that schedule should be and how it should be sold.

You want to hear which schedule they recommend, what it costs the client it does not suit, and how the company should market the promise that comes with it. During the presentation you are to ask the following questions of the participant team:
judgeQuestions: Which approach did you rule out, and what would we have gained by taking it instead?
If we had kept both schedules running side by side, what would that have cost us?
